Two opening questions take their force from legal shape, and Henry works each. A husband could put away a wife on any slight disgust, but the writ went into the woman's own hand, so let them produce it; a father could sell children to creditors, but God owed nothing to the powers they were sold to. Hence his rule, that God chastens neither for pleasure nor profit, and his turn of the charge: they were sold not as children by parents clearing a debt but as criminals by judges punishing a crime. Ellicott adds that this wife was never formally repudiated as her sister was, and no creditor could claim her children; divorce and sale were her own acts.

The unanswered coming is read at different widths. Delitzsch names one radical sin behind the exile, disobedience to the word, which brought the banishment and made it last. Ellicott will not narrow the coming to one occasion, taking in the release from captivity, the promise of more, and the fullest sense in and through the Servant, none arriving to help or to receive the message. Henry fills that out historically, prophets sent early and mocked, last of all the Son who came to his own; when God calls men to happiness and they will not answer, they are left miserable justly. Clarke reads the fish as dried up rather than stinking, on a manuscript and the Greek. Over the blackened heavens Gill offers three referents, the darkness in Egypt, ordinary tempest, and the dark at the crucifixion; Wesley sees sackcloth drawn to save a people.

Who speaks from the fourth verse on is the chapter's real division, and each reader takes a position. Gill denies the prophetic reference outright, naming Aben Ezra and Kimchi for it. Clarke goes as far the other way, granting the chapter has been understood of the prophet but insisting it speaks more clearly of Jesus of Nazareth than of the son of Amos. Henry keeps both, the prophet saying something of himself and then speaking as a type. Wesley allows the prophet in some sort but thinks the words meant directly of Christ. Ellicott makes it a soliloquy of the Servant, allowing echoes of the prophet's experience in it. Delitzsch identifies the speaker with the one in whom God had come to the nation.

The gifts described are given a schoolroom sense. Ellicott renders the tongue as a disciple's, and the work not as speech generally but as sustaining the weary with a word; the morning waking he hears as a deliberate contrast with the dreams and night visions of lesser inspiration. Delitzsch notes that the word is the older form of the later term for pupils and stands at both ends of the verse, an instance of the mirroring favoured throughout. Henry draws the ministerial moral from the pairing of tongue and ear: none should teach who have not first learned, the best learning being to know how to speak to troubled consciences. Gill agrees, putting knowledge of the weary case first among a minister's gifts.

The obedience is read backwards from its cost. Gill hears in the opened ear the bored ear of a servant who would not go free; Clarke observes that eleven manuscripts, the oldest edition and two versions prefix a conjunction to the clause about drawing back. Delitzsch takes the verb for rebellion in its root sense of stiffening oneself, and says the sufferer was never inwardly overcome. On the indignities Clarke assembles his fullest note: plucking the beard as the gravest insult possible, and spitting as detestation so extreme that among Medes and Persians it offended in a man's mere presence. He records the learned doubt whether the older passages mean more than spitting on the ground, and overrules it here on the Gospel's reference. Gill names Pilate; Wesley says only that he yielded himself up.

The turn from suffering to confidence rests on one support, and Ellicott says so in a line: that single stay gives the sufferer an indomitable strength. Clarke reaches for the nearest parallel, a forehead made adamant, harder than rock against a rebellious house. Gill pauses over what a promise of help implies: a helped Redeemer is no contradiction of his deity, the words being spoken of him as man, crucified through weakness, and the need shows how great the work was, no mere creature being able to effect it.

The passage is staged as a trial, and the readers keep the vocabulary. Delitzsch pairs the two verbs as forensic opposites, setting a man forth as righteous or guilty. Ellicott renders the adversary literally, the master of a lawsuit, the prosecutor, and describes an appeal from unrighteous earthly judges to one who judges righteously, so the accuser ceases to matter. Clarke restores from a Bodleian manuscript a word he thinks dropped from the text. Wesley makes the vindication public, cleared by many and mighty signs; Gill locates it in resurrection, ascension, and the gifts given after. Delitzsch adds the fate of the opposition, who carry the germ of their destruction and wear out like a garment under the moth.

Then comes the verse Clarke says has been generally and dangerously misunderstood. It has been preached, he complains, to prove a man may sincerely fear God and obey his servant's voice and still walk without light or sense of approval; he calls that impossible on the word of Christ that his follower shall not walk in darkness. His remedy is Lowth's redistribution: two questions, each with its answer. Who fears the LORD? Let him hearken to the voice of his servant. Who walks in darkness without light? Let him trust in the name of the LORD and prop himself on his God. The Greek and Syriac support it, reading the participle as a verb, which gives a far more elegant turn to the sentence. Where some continually write bitter things against themselves under a morbid melancholy, the word of God should not be bent down to their state.

Everyone else takes the reading he rejects. Henry describes the very case: one who has the fear of God and faith in Christ and yet for a time no light — evidences clouded, joy interrupted, the Spirit's testimony suspended, the light of God's countenance eclipsed. He grants that pensive Christians are melancholy and those who fear apt to fear too much, and prescribes the two clauses as one cure, running into the name as into a strong tower and staying oneself on the covenant. Ellicott goes further, hearing what every true servant knows, quoting the prayer of Ajax for light even if it be light to die by, and setting the cry of dereliction and the commending of the spirit as darkness and trust. Wesley draws the line that makes the reading defensible: the darkness is misery, not sin. Gill distinguishes filial fear from slavish; Delitzsch marks where the servant's words end.

The closing fire is read three ways. Gill and Wesley keep it plain, the given light rejected and reason, tradition, or one's own righteousness set up instead. Henry sharpens the last into a picture: sacrifice offered with fire of one's own striking rather than fire from heaven, as two priests once did, worldly comforts being sparks that warm while they last. Clarke offers a general sense, human policy without faith; a particular one from Vitringa, the factions who stirred up the war that burned their own city; and a third for the presumptuous who would think it criminal to doubt their salvation. Ellicott keeps both standard senses, wrath and earthly ease, notes that many render the clause as girding oneself with firebrands, calumnies for weapons, and takes the lying down in sorrow to point beyond death.
